source.title: Summit: Scaling Deep Learning Interpretability by Visualizing Activation and Attribution Summarizations
source.authors: Fred Hohman; Haekyu Park; Caleb Robinson; Duen Horng Chau

record.tranche_reason: The study builds and presents attribution-graph explanations from a vision model’s own channels, extending this kind of neuron-based explanation to Inception V1. Its qualitative case studies bear on whether such graphs can explain model behavior, but it does not evaluate explanation fidelity or compare against a replacement model.
record.gate_note: The study reports qualitative attribution-graph findings for Inception V1 classes and channels, recorded below. It does not measure neuron-pole job shares, test explanations on held-out activations, score explanations automatically, or evaluate the InceptionV1 cat-and-car pose example. The 3%, 5-channel, and 7.5% settings are method parameters, not outcome rows; cited findings from other work are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: Summit builds channel-level attribution graphs for Inception V1 and presents qualitative case studies. It never measures how well the graphs explain or predict model behaviour. There is no fidelity, ablation or completeness test and no comparison with a replacement model or its reconstruction error. The paper shows the method's outputs rather than testing whether neurons suffice as circuit units. It reports no neuron-job shares, held-out activation prediction or automated explanation scores.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors present Summit as a scalable, interactive way to summarize which features Inception V1 learns per class and how they connect, illustrated by qualitative exploration scenarios. They list automated channel-quality measures, other architectures and better attribution methods as future work.
record.recipe_differences: Summit aggregates maximum channel activations and inter-layer influences over ImageNet classes, then uses Personalized PageRank to extract attribution graphs. It does not use the language-model neuron-explanation procedure or test explanations on held-out activations.

fits_no_version.finding: Channel-level attribution graphs (activation and influence aggregation plus Personalized PageRank) give human-readable class summaries in Inception V1, e.g. tench relying on person and hand features. They also surface 5 non-semantic channels that had to be excluded by hand.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Aggregated attribution graphs built from a vision CNN's own channels yield qualitatively interpretable class-level circuits. A few channels are non-semantic and need manual exclusion.

record.problems: The evidence on explanation quality is qualitative and based on selected case studies. The paper reports no independent fidelity or causal validation of the graph interpretations, no uncertainty estimates, and no automated measure of channel semantic quality; it says 5 non-semantic channels were excluded manually.

untested.parts: Whether neuron-built attribution graphs explain behaviour: no fidelity, ablation, reconstruction-error or replacement-model comparison. The model is a 2014 CNN, not a large language model.
Shares across language models and scale.
The cat-and-car pose neuron and recursive generalization versus superposition.
How the interpretable share varies with tools or architecture.
Prediction of firing from explanations based on activating examples.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T3' and its V5 labels are rejected. The paper presents qualitative tool demonstrations without any measure of explanatory sufficiency, so none of its rows can support or limit V5. The hyperparameter settings (3%, 5 channels, 7.5%) are correctly left out as rows.

versions.untested_parts: Neuron-pole shares and the proportion of single-job, two-job, or not-understood poles.
Comparisons across language models, dense and mixture-of-experts models, or model scale up to trillions of parameters.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose as a shared feature, and recursive generalization versus superposition.
Whether architecture, regularization, and tools explain messy late-layer neurons, or the stated estimates of interpretable-neuron shares for InceptionV1-sized vision models.

The study presents qualitative graph-based explanations from the model’s own channels, but does not quantify explanation fidelity, measure reconstruction error, or compare with a trained replacement model.
Whether explanations based on activating examples predict where neurons fire on separate activations.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

rows.subject: Inception V1
rows.operation_detail: Generated an attribution graph for the tench class from aggregated channel activations and influences; inspected graph channels and dataset patches.
rows.measure: Qualitative features and associations represented in the class attribution graph.
rows.value: The graph showed people-related features in earlier layers and fish-body and scale detectors in a middle layer; dataset patches showed people holding fish. The authors report that the model used people detectors together with brown fish-body and scale detectors for the class.
rows.note: Qualitative interpretation from the graph and dataset examples; the study does not independently validate whether these features are causally necessary.
rows.check: This is a qualitative tench graph story with no measure of whether the graph explains the prediction. It cannot show V5's sufficiency claim.

rows.subject: Inception V1
rows.operation_detail: Generated and inspected an attribution graph for the lionfish class.
rows.measure: Qualitative features and associations represented in the class attribution graph.
rows.value: The graph had few fish-part detectors and many texture features, including stripes and quills; a final-layer orange-fish feature was influenced by stripe and quill detectors. The authors report no people object detectors in the graph.
rows.note: Qualitative graph interpretation; no external fidelity or causal validation is reported.
rows.check: This is a qualitative lionfish graph interpretation with no fidelity or causal test.

rows.subject: Inception V1
rows.operation_detail: Inspected the horsecart class across layer embeddings and its attribution graph.

conditions.value: early, middle, and final convolutional layers

rows.measure: Qualitative class associations and graph features.
rows.value: The class was associated with mechanical classes in early layers, animal classes in middle layers, and mechanical classes again at the final convolutional layer. Its graph included people, spoke wheels, horse hips, and horse bodies with saddles and mechanical gear.
rows.note: The layer association shifts are reported from the embedding view; graph inspection supplies the listed component features.
rows.check: This is an embedding-neighbour shift and graph features for horsecart. It describes the tool's output and is not a test of explanation sufficiency.

rows.subject: Inception V1
rows.operation_detail: Compared the intersection of attribution graphs for black bear and brown bear.
rows.measure: Qualitative shared and discriminating features in the graphs.
rows.value: The graphs shared bear-related features and diverged toward the output with fur-color and face-color features distinguishing the classes.
rows.note: The authors say the distinction aligns with how humans might classify bears; no human comparison study is reported.
rows.check: This is a qualitative comparison of the bear-class graphs. The human alignment is asserted, not measured.

rows.subject: Inception V1
rows.operation_detail: Inspected channels using Summit and manually checked non-semantic channels across classes.
rows.measure: Number and examples of channels reported to detect irrelevant features.
rows.value: 5 total non-semantic channels were found: mixed3a 67, mixed3a 190, mixed3b 390, mixed3b 399, and mixed3b 412. The authors excluded them and reran aggregation for the graphs.
rows.note: This shows a limitation in the graph workflow: the authors say Summit does not automatically measure channels’ semantic quality and manually excluded these channels.
rows.check: It counts 5 non-semantic early-layer channels that were excluded manually. This is a pipeline-cleaning step, not a test of V5, and not a share of interpretable neurons (no denominator is reported).

rows.subject: Inception V1
rows.operation_detail: Inspected attribution graphs for classes with few important middle-layer channels.
rows.measure: Qualitative number and apparent class relevance of important channels.
rows.value: The authors observed only a few important middle-layer channels and suggested they could contain enough information to act as a predictor for the class.
rows.note: The proposed predictor is a suggestion; the study does not test it.
rows.check: It records an untested suggestion that a few middle-layer channels could act as a zebra predictor. It is an observation for future design, not a result.

rows.subject: Inception V1
rows.operation_detail: Inspected attribution graphs for classes with few important middle-layer channels.
rows.measure: Qualitative number and apparent class relevance of important channels.
rows.value: The authors observed only a few important middle-layer channels and suggested they could contain enough information to act as a predictor for the class.
rows.note: The proposed predictor is a suggestion; the study does not test it.
rows.check: It records the same untested suggestion for green mamba. It is not a result bearing on any version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Qualitative attribution-graph case studies on Inception V1 ImageNet classes
reader_labels.reason: The graphs yield reported feature and association interpretations for the tench, lionfish, horsecart, and bear classes without a replacement model (R1–R4).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Channel semantic quality in the reported graph workflow
reader_labels.reason: The authors found 5 non-semantic channels, excluded them manually, and state that Summit does not automatically measure semantic quality (R5).
